claims.claim: H104K-HSPB5 has the largest average diameter, 17 nm.
claims.source: The size distribution derived in this way is consistent with the SEC-MALS analysis: WT-HSPB5 at pH 7.5 has the smallest average diameter, 15 nm, (a range of 13–17 nm), H104K-HSPB5 has the largest, with an average of 17 nm, and WT-HSPB5 at pH 6.5 is intermediate, at 16 nm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM 2D projection averages.

claims.claim: WT-HSPB5 at pH 6.5 has an intermediate average diameter of 16 nm.
claims.source: The size distribution derived in this way is consistent with the SEC-MALS analysis: WT-HSPB5 at pH 7.5 has the smallest average diameter, 15 nm, (a range of 13–17 nm), H104K-HSPB5 has the largest, with an average of 17 nm, and WT-HSPB5 at pH 6.5 is intermediate, at 16 nm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM 2D projection averages.

claims.claim: The diameter of the WT-HSPB5 cryo-EM model determined similarly from the circular average measures 15 nm, in good agreement with our measurements.
claims.source: For comparison, the diameter of the WT-HSPB5 cryo-EM model (Braun et al., 2011) determined similarly from the circular average measures 15 nm, in good agreement with our measurements.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previously published structural data.

claims.claim: Conditions and/or mutations that affect the stability of the antiparallel dimer interface have substantial impact on HSPB5 oligomer size and structure.
claims.source: Altogether the results reveal that conditions and/or mutations that affect the stability of the antiparallel dimer interface have substantial impact on HSPB5 oligomer size and structure.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the SEC-MALS and EM data.

claims.claim: At pH 7.5, H104Q- and H104K-HSPB5 are more effective than WT-HSPB5 at delaying formation of large aggregates by two model clients, αLactalbumin (αLac) destabilized by addition of DTT, and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) destabilized by addition of DTT and EDTA.
claims.source: At pH 7.5, H104Q- and H104K-HSPB5 are more effective than WT-HSPB5 at delaying formation of large aggregates by two model clients, αLactalbumin (αLac) destabilized by addition of DTT, and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) destabilized by addition of DTT and EDTA (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by holdase assay data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Enhanced holdase activity is associated with destabilization of the dimer interface.
claims.source: The results indicate that enhanced holdase activity is associated with destabilization of the dimer interface.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the holdase assay results for mutants.

claims.claim: Although WT-HSPB5 maintains αLac in a soluble form during the time frame of the experiment, no interaction between the two proteins was detected by SEC or SDS-PAGE, indicating that its holdase function is achieved through highly transient interactions.
claims.source: Although WT-HSPB5 maintains αLac in a soluble form during the time frame of the experiment, no interaction between the two proteins was detected by SEC or SDS-PAGE, indicating that its holdase function is achieved through highly transient interactions (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS and SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: A mixture of αLac and H104K-HSPB5 elutes with a dramatically different profile, with a broad peak that elutes between 7.5 and 9.2 ml containing both proteins.
claims.source: In contrast, a mixture of αLac and H104K-HSPB5 elutes with a dramatically different profile. SDS-PAGE analysis across the broad peak that elutes between 7.5 and 9.2 ml shows that it contains both proteins (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS and SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: There is a broad range of molecular weights across the H104K-HSPB5/αLac peak, from >550 kDa to ∼250 kDa.
claims.source: There is a broad range of molecular weights across this peak, from >550 kDa to ∼250 kDa.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS measurements.

claims.claim: Long-lived complexes are formed between αLac and the H104 mutant HSPB5s, and these are markedly smaller than the oligomers that are populated in the absence of client protein.
claims.source: Thus, long-lived complexes are formed between αLac and the H104 mutant HSPB5s, and these are markedly smaller than the oligomers that are populated in the absence of client protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on SEC-MALS data comparing oligomers with and without client.

claims.claim: The mutant HSPB5/αLac complexes remain stable following dilution for EM.
claims.source: In micrograph and single particle images, the particles appear intact and there is little background from unbound protein, indicating the mutant HSPB5/αLac complexes remain stable following dilution for EM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from EM images.

claims.claim: The particles in H104K-HSPB5/αLac complexes are much smaller and are structurally distinct from the spherical oligomers observed for WT-, H104Q-, or H104K-HSPB5 on their own.
claims.source: The particles are much smaller and are structurally distinct from the spherical oligomers observed for WT-, H104Q-, or H104K-HSPB5 on their own.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from EM images comparing complexes with oligomers alone.

claims.claim: A major structural reorganization occurs in the mutant sHSP upon binding of a model client protein.
claims.source: The 2D averages (Figure 7D) show clear structural features and reveal that a major structural reorganization occurs in the mutant sHSP upon binding of a model client protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on EM 2D projection averages shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: No smaller species were detected in unfractionated samples of mixtures of WT-HSPB5 and α-Lac analyzed by negative stain EM, and the spherical oligomers remain unchanged for WT-HSPB5.
claims.source: To see if similar HSPB5/αLac complexes form with WT-HSPB5 but do not survive the SEC-MALS experiment, unfractionated samples of mixtures of WT-HSPB5 and α-Lac were analyzed by negative stain EM (data not shown). No smaller species were detected and the spherical oligomers remain unchanged for WT-HSPB5.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from EM experiments.

claims.claim: HSPB5 oligomers with destabilized dimer interfaces disassemble and undergo a dramatic reorganization to form stable complexes with a model client protein while the wild-type protein at pH 7.5 does not do so and performs its holdase function via highly transient interactions with client.
claims.source: Overall the results demonstrate that HSPB5 oligomers with destabilized dimer interfaces disassemble and undergo a dramatic reorganization to form stable complexes with a model client protein while the wild-type protein at pH 7.5 does not do so and performs its holdase function via highly transient interactions with client.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the client binding experiments.

claims.claim: HSPB5-ACD dimers dissociate into folded monomers that are favored as the pH decreases.
claims.source: We find that HSPB5-ACD dimers dissociate into folded monomers that are favored as the pH decreases.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the ITC and NMR findings.

claims.claim: ITC and NMR measurements revealed a modest affinity for the ACD dimer (KD of 36 μM at pH 7.5, 37°C), with dimers dissociating at a rate of 400 s−1.
claims.source: ITC and NMR measurements revealed a modest affinity for the ACD dimer (KD of 36 μM at pH 7.5, 37°C), with dimers dissociating at a rate of 400 s−1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the ITC and NMR relaxation dispersion findings.

claims.claim: The juxtaposition of Glu-117 and Glu-117′ in the middle of the interface and the positively and negatively charged patches that cross the interface may contribute to the modest affinity and to the dynamics and plasticity observed in the interface.
claims.source: The juxtaposition of Glu-117 and Glu-117′ in the middle of the interface and the positively and negatively charged patches that cross the interface may contribute to the modest affinity and to the dynamics and plasticity we observed in the interface.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural features.

claims.claim: Dimer affinity decreases 15-fold over 1 pH unit (pH 7.5 to pH 6.5) and this likely corresponds to a similar fold increase in the rate of dissociation at the dimer interface.
claims.source: Dimer affinity decreases 15-fold over 1 pH unit (pH 7.5 to pH 6.5) and this likely corresponds to a similar fold increase in the rate of dissociation at the dimer interface.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the measured KD values at different pH.

claims.claim: A pH-dependent destabilization of the HSPB5-ACD dimer interface was inferred from native MS studies performed on oligomers as a function of pH.
claims.source: A pH-dependent destabilization of the HSPB5-ACD dimer interface was inferred from native MS studies performed on oligomers as a function of pH; our results offer a direct confirmation and quantification of this hypothesis (Baldwin et al., 2011b).
claims.evidence: This claim references previous work and states that the current results confirm it.

claims.claim: Substitution of His-104 with Gln or Lys decreases dimer stability substantially.
claims.source: We identified a histidine residue that plays a key role in ACD dimer interface stability. Substitution of His-104 with Gln or Lys decreases dimer stability substantially.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the mutagenesis and NMR findings.

claims.claim: Among the ten human sHSPs, His-104 is the most conserved His residue, appearing in eight of ten proteins, with the non-H104-containing sHSPs having a Gln (HSPB9) or a Lys (HSPB7).
claims.source: Among the ten human sHSPs, His-104 is the most conserved His residue, appearing in eight of ten proteins, with the non-H104-containing sHSPs having a Gln (HSPB9) or a Lys (HSPB7) (Figure 1—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: The unusual tautomeric state adopted by His-104 in HSPB5 is also observed for the analogous histidines in HSPB1 (His-124) and HSPB6 (His-103).
claims.source: Consistent with a conserved role for His-104, the unusual tautomeric state adopted by His-104 in HSPB5 is also observed for the analogous histidines in HSPB1 (His-124) and HSPB6 (His-103) (Rajagopal and Klevit, unpublished observation).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claims.claim: His-104 is located at the beginning of Loop 5/6, the loop connecting strands β5 and the dimer interface strand, β6+7.
claims.source: His-104 is located at the beginning of Loop 5/6, the loop connecting strands β5 and the dimer interface strand, β6+7 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a structural observation from the NMR structure.

claims.claim: Residues in Loop 5/6 have similar exchange rates to dimer interface residues, suggesting that loop movements and the structural transition may be coupled.
claims.source: Residues in Loop 5/6 have similar exchange rates suggesting that loop movements and the structural transition may be coupled.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on similar exchange rates.

claims.claim: His-111 at the apex of Loop 5/6 makes contacts to Arg-120' and Tyr-122' across the dimer interface.
claims.source: Nevertheless, consistent with this notion, inter-subunit contacts are observed that involve Loop 5/6 residues: His-111 at the apex of Loop 5/6 makes contacts to Arg-120' and Tyr-122' across the dimer interface.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the NMR structure.

claims.claim: A possible consequence of His-104 protonation is to alter the conformation or position of Loop 5/6, disrupting inter-subunit contacts involving the loop and shifting the dimer–monomer equilibrium of the HSPB5-ACD.
claims.source: A possible consequence of His-104 protonation, which sits at the base of the loop, is to alter the conformation or position of Loop 5/6, disrupting inter-subunit contacts involving the loop and shifting the dimer–monomer equilibrium of the HSPB5-ACD.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal.

claims.claim: In both loop conformations His-104 sits at the center of a dynamic network of electrostatic and H-bonding interactions that is responsible for modulating the stability of the dimer interface.
claims.source: In sum, we propose that in both loop conformations His-104 sits at the center of a dynamic network of electrostatic and H-bonding interactions that is responsible for modulating the stability of the dimer interface.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: A survey of all 17 available mammalian sHSP-ACD structures reveals that Loop 5/6 is found in two conformations; a 'loop up' conformation and a 'loop down' conformation.
claims.source: A survey of all 17 available mammalian sHSP-ACD structures (9 HSPB5 [WT and mutants], 3 HSPB1, and 3 HSPB6) reveals that Loop 5/6 is found in two conformations; a 'loop up' conformation as seen in the HSPB5-ACD solution structure and a 'loop down' conformation.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of multiple published structures.

claims.claim: In the 'loop up' structures, the residues corresponding to His-111, Asp-109, and Arg-120 are involved in inter-subunit contacts in all cases.
claims.source: In the 'loop up' structures, the details of the interactions between Loop 5/6 residues across the dimer interface vary, again pointing to the plasticity of this region. Nevertheless, the residues corresponding to His-111, Asp-109, and Arg-120 are involved in all cases.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of multiple published structures.

claims.claim: Loop 5/6 is remarkably well conserved among the human sHSPs.
claims.source: Furthermore, although Loop 5/6 contains predominantly polar and/or charged residues, it is remarkably well conserved among the human sHSPs (Figure 1—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: In HSPB5, residues His-104, Asp-109, and His-111 have recently been implicated in Cu2+ and Zn2+ binding and the binding of divalent cation appears to destabilize the dimer interface.
claims.source: In HSPB5, residues His-104, Asp-109, and His-111 have recently been implicated in Cu2+ and Zn2+ binding and the binding of divalent cation appears to destabilize the dimer interface (Mainz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: In HSPB1, substitution of the two glutamate residues that correspond to HSPB5 Glu-105 and Glu-106 to Ala resulted in monomeric HSPB1-ACD.
claims.source: In HSPB1, which has an almost identical Loop 5/6 sequence to HSPB5, substitution of the two glutamate residues that correspond to HSPB5 Glu-105 and Glu-106 to Ala resulted in monomeric HSPB1-ACD (Baranova et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: A Loop 5/6 mutation in HSPB1, R127W (corresponding to Arg107 in HSPB5 numbering) is reported to promote monomer over dimer.
claims.source: Also, a Loop 5/6 mutation in HSPB1, R127W (corresponding to Arg107 in HSPB5 numbering) is reported to promote monomer over dimer (Almeida-Souza et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: In each case, a change in the net charge of Loop 5/6 leads to monomer being more favored.
claims.source: In each case, a change in the net charge of Loop 5/6 leads to monomer being more favored.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the examples cited.

claims.claim: Properties of Loop 5/6 are coupled to the stability of the dimer interface.
claims.source: Altogether the observations suggest a model in which properties of Loop 5/6 are coupled to the stability of the dimer interface.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on multiple observations.

claims.claim: Inheritance of single alleles of D109H-HSPB5 or R127W-HSPB1 is associated with cataract, myofibrillar myopathy, and distal hereditary motor neuropathy.
claims.source: It is notable that inheritance of single alleles of D109H-HSPB5 or R127W-HSPB1 is associated with cataract, myofibrillar myopathy, and distal hereditary motor neuropathy (Nefedova et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Both D109H-HSPB5 and R127W-HSPB1 mutations alter the net charge of Loop 5/6, implying a critical role for structural and/or dynamic properties of Loop 5/6 in sHSP function.
claims.source: Both mutations alter the net charge of Loop 5/6, implying a critical role for structural and/or dynamic properties of Loop 5/6 in sHSP function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the disease-associated mutations.

claims.claim: Decreasing pH or substituting His-104 has dramatic effects on oligomer dimensions and subunit stoichiometry.
claims.source: Moving into the context of full-length HSPB5, we found that decreasing pH or substituting His-104 has dramatic effects on oligomer dimensions and subunit stoichiometry.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the SEC-MALS and EM findings.

claims.claim: A continuum of oligomer sizes is observed that trends reciprocally with ACD dimer interface stability.
claims.source: A continuum of oligomer sizes is observed that trends reciprocally with ACD dimer interface stability.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the oligomer size data for different conditions and mutants.

claims.claim: H104K-HSPB5, whose ACD will be predominantly monomeric, assembles into the largest oligomers containing over 40 subunits.
claims.source: H104K-HSPB5, whose ACD will be predominantly monomeric, assembles into the largest oligomers containing over 40 subunits.
claims.evidence: This is based on SEC-MALS measurements and inference about the ACD state.

claims.claim: While the notion that dimers are the fundamental building blocks of sHSP oligomers may describe the situation under certain conditions, oligomers can also be built from monomeric subunits and from combinations of dimeric and monomeric units.
claims.source: While the notion that dimers are the fundamental building blocks of sHSP oligomers may describe the situation under certain conditions, our results indicate that oligomers can also be built from monomeric subunits and from combinations of dimeric and monomeric units and that more monomeric subunits can be incorporated into a given oligomer.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the oligomer size data.

claims.claim: More monomeric subunits can be incorporated into a given oligomer.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the oligomer size data.

claims.claim: This revelation will be important in any future attempts to determine HSPB5 oligomer structures for oligomers larger than the 24-mer previously determined.

claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings for future work.

claims.claim: The His-104 mutants allowed asking if and how the dimer interface contributes to holdase function without the confounding complications of comparing aggregation of model denatured client proteins at differing pHs.
claims.source: The His-104 mutants allowed us to ask if and how the dimer interface contributes to holdase function without the confounding complications of comparing aggregation of model denatured client proteins at differing pHs.
claims.evidence: This describes the rationale for using the mutants.

claims.claim: Both dimer-destabilizing mutations yield an HSPB5 that can delay aggregation of model clients longer than the wild-type protein at pH 7.5.
claims.source: Both dimer-destabilizing mutations yield an HSPB5 that can delay aggregation of model clients longer than the wild-type protein at pH 7.5.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the holdase assay results.

claims.claim: The His-104 mutant proteins, which form much larger oligomers than WT-HSPB5, reorganize to form long-lived complexes with a client protein.

results.result: The solution NMR structure of HSPB5-ACD at pH 7.5 reveals a conserved β-sandwich fold with dimers formed through antiparallel β6+7 strands. Loop 5/6 exhibits conformational plasticity, adopting both 'up' and 'down' conformations across different structures at physiological pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C24 collectively describe the NMR structure determination and structural features of HSPB5-ACD. The structure was determined using appropriate NMR data (NOEs, RDCs, chemical shifts) and shows consistency with previous structures while revealing Loop 5/6 plasticity. The structural observations are well-supported by the experimental data presented.

results.result: NMR relaxation measurements reveal that the HSPB5-ACD dimer undergoes millisecond timescale dynamics, with the dimer interface and Loop 5/6 exchanging between major and minor species at rates of 760-1119 s⁻¹. The protomer structure remains stable over a wide pH range while the dimer interface and Loop 5/6 exhibit plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 describe NMR relaxation dispersion experiments that characterize dynamics in HSPB5-ACD. The data show appropriate fitting to two-state models and identify specific regions undergoing exchange. The experimental approach is sound and the conclusions about structural plasticity are well-supported by the relaxation data.

results.result: ITC measurements demonstrate pH-dependent destabilization of the HSPB5-ACD dimer, with KD values of 2 ± 2 μM at pH 7.5 and 30 ± 16 μM at pH 6.5 (25°C). Temperature increase to 37°C also destabilizes the dimer (KD = 36 ± 2 μM at pH 7.5).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 present ITC measurements of dimer stability under different conditions. The data fit a simple dimer-monomer equilibrium model and show good agreement with independent MS measurements (C37). The experimental design is appropriate and the conclusions about pH and temperature effects are well-supported. Error bars are provided for the measurements.

results.result: pH titration monitored by NMR spectroscopy reveals that HSPB5-ACD undergoes a slow-exchange transition below pH 6.7, with chemical shift perturbations concentrated at the dimer interface and Loop 5/6. The minor species detected by relaxation dispersion at pH 7.5 corresponds to the monomeric form populated at lower pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C49 describe pH-dependent NMR spectroscopy experiments that identify a dimer-to-monomer transition. The peak doubling behavior, chemical shift perturbations, and correspondence between relaxation dispersion predictions and pH titration data provide strong converging evidence. The population estimates from relaxation dispersion (~5%) agree well with ITC predictions (4%).

results.result: Concentration-dependent relaxation dispersion measurements at 37°C reveal that the HSPB5-ACD dimer dissociates at a rate of 400 s⁻¹, with diffusion-controlled association (kmd = 1.1 × 10⁷ M⁻¹ s⁻¹). This rate is orders of magnitude faster than full-length HSPB5 subunit exchange (10⁻³ s⁻¹), suggesting dimer interfaces break and reform many times during subunit residency in oligomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 present kinetic analysis of dimer dissociation and compare it to oligomer subunit exchange. The concentration dependence confirms the dimer-monomer mechanism, and the calculated rate constants are consistent with diffusion-controlled association. The comparison with published subunit exchange rates (C54) supports the inference about interface dynamics within oligomers, though C56 is somewhat speculative.

results.result: HSPB5-ACD contains five histidine residues (5.6% of sequence) concentrated near the dimer center. His-104 adopts an unusual Nδ1H tautomer stabilized by hydrogen bonding, with its backbone resonance behavior indicating sensitivity to the dimer-monomer transition despite not being on the interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C65 characterize the histidine residues in HSPB5-ACD using NMR. The pKR measurements, tautomeric state determination, and chemical shift analysis are appropriate methods. The identification of His-104's unusual tautomeric state and H-bonding is well-supported by the NMR data, though the specific H-bonding partner cannot be definitively identified from the ensemble (C64).

results.result: His-104 mutations dramatically destabilize the HSPB5-ACD dimer: H104Q shows equal dimer/monomer populations at pH 7.5 (estimated KD ~100-500 μM), while H104K is predominantly monomeric (estimated KD >1 mM), representing >100-fold destabilization. Other histidine mutations do not show this effect, identifying His-104 as a specific hotspot controlling dimer stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C74 present mutagenesis data demonstrating His-104's critical role in dimer stability. The NMR spectra clearly show the different oligomeric states of the mutants. While the KD estimates (C70-C71) are order-of-magnitude approximations based on peak intensities rather than direct measurements, they are reasonable given the experimental constraints. The specificity is confirmed by control mutations of other histidines (C73).

results.result: SEC-MALS and EM measurements show that WT-HSPB5 oligomers expand with decreasing pH, from an average of ~24 subunits (465 kDa, 15 nm diameter) at pH 7.5 to ~36 subunits (720 kDa, 16 nm diameter) at pH 6.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 present complementary SEC-MALS and EM data characterizing pH-dependent oligomer expansion. The measurements are consistent between techniques and confirm previous reports (C75). The data are quantitative with appropriate replication. The structural observations from EM support the size measurements from SEC-MALS.

results.result: His-104 mutations produce larger oligomers: H104K-HSPB5 forms the largest oligomers (~41 subunits, 810 kDa, 17 nm diameter) while H104Q is intermediate. Mixing experiments show that oligomer size titrates with the ratio of WT to H104K subunits, consistent with oligomers assembled from combinations of dimeric and monomeric building blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 demonstrate that dimer destabilization leads to larger oligomers. The SEC-MALS data are clear and the mixing experiments (C85) provide strong support for the model that oligomers can incorporate both dimeric and monomeric units. However, C84 and C86 involve some speculation about the exact composition of oligomers, as direct structural evidence for monomer vs. dimer incorporation is not provided.

results.result: Quantitative EM analysis reveals a size distribution consistent with SEC-MALS: WT-HSPB5 at pH 7.5 has the smallest average diameter (15 nm), H104K-HSPB5 the largest (17 nm), and WT at pH 6.5 is intermediate (16 nm). The measurements agree with previous cryo-EM models.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 present quantitative EM analysis that corroborates the SEC-MALS findings. The size measurements are systematic and show internal consistency. The agreement with published cryo-EM data (C91) provides external validation. The experiments were performed in triplicate, providing appropriate replication.

results.result: His-104 mutants (H104Q and H104K) show enhanced holdase activity compared to WT-HSPB5 at pH 7.5, delaying aggregation of model client proteins (αLac and ADH) more effectively. This enhanced activity is associated with dimer interface destabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 present holdase assay data showing that dimer destabilization enhances chaperone activity. The assays were performed in duplicate with two different client proteins, providing appropriate replication and generalizability. The inference linking enhanced activity to dimer destabilization (C94) is reasonable given the correlation, though the mechanism is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: WT-HSPB5 maintains client proteins soluble through transient interactions that are undetectable by SEC or EM, while His-104 mutants form long-lived, stable complexes with clients that are smaller (250-550 kDa) than the mutant oligomers alone. EM reveals that mutant HSPB5 undergoes major structural reorganization upon client binding, forming structurally distinct complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C104 demonstrate fundamentally different client-binding mechanisms for WT vs. mutant HSPB5. The SEC-MALS and EM data clearly show stable complexes for mutants but not WT. The structural reorganization is evident in the EM images. The control experiment (C103) confirms that WT does not form similar complexes. This is a key mechanistic finding revealing a cryptic mode of chaperone action.

results.result: HSPB5-ACD dimers dissociate into folded monomers with modest affinity (KD = 36 μM at pH 7.5, 37°C) and a dissociation rate of 400 s⁻¹. Dimer affinity decreases 15-fold over one pH unit (pH 7.5 to 6.5), confirming previous inferences from native MS studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 summarize the key thermodynamic and kinetic findings. The measurements are well-supported by the ITC and NMR data. C107 is somewhat speculative about the structural basis for modest affinity, but is a reasonable interpretation. C109 appropriately acknowledges that the current work confirms and quantifies previous inferences.

results.result: His-104, the most conserved histidine among human sHSPs, is located at the base of Loop 5/6 and adopts an unusual tautomeric state conserved in HSPB1 and HSPB6. His-104 sits at the center of a dynamic network of electrostatic and H-bonding interactions that modulate dimer stability, possibly through coupling Loop 5/6 movements to the dimer interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C117 synthesize findings about His-104's structural role and evolutionary conservation. The conservation analysis (C111) and tautomeric state observations (C112) are data-supported. The mechanistic proposals (C114, C116, C117) are reasonable inferences based on the structural data and relaxation measurements, though they remain somewhat speculative. The inter-subunit contacts involving Loop 5/6 (C115) support the coupling hypothesis.

results.result: Survey of 17 mammalian sHSP-ACD structures reveals Loop 5/6 adopts two conformations with conserved inter-subunit contacts involving His-111, Asp-109, and Arg-120. Multiple studies show that mutations altering Loop 5/6 charge favor monomer over dimer, suggesting Loop 5/6 properties are coupled to dimer interface stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C125 present comparative structural analysis and cite multiple independent studies showing Loop 5/6's role in dimer stability. The structural survey is appropriate and the cited examples (C121-C123) from the literature support the general principle. C125 is a reasonable inference based on the convergent evidence, though it represents a model rather than direct proof of coupling.

results.result: Disease-associated mutations D109H-HSPB5 and R127W-HSPB1, which alter Loop 5/6 charge, are linked to cataract, myofibrillar myopathy, and neuropathy, implying a critical role for Loop 5/6 properties in sHSP function.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 cite established disease associations and make a reasonable inference about the functional importance of Loop 5/6. The citation supports the disease associations (C126), and the inference (C127) is logical given the current findings about Loop 5/6's role in dimer stability. However, the exact mechanism by which these mutations cause disease is not established.

results.result: Decreasing pH or His-104 mutation produces a continuum of oligomer sizes that trends reciprocally with dimer stability. H104K-HSPB5 assembles into the largest oligomers (>40 subunits), suggesting oligomers can be built from monomeric subunits or combinations of dimeric and monomeric units, challenging the notion that dimers are always the fundamental building blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132 present a revised model of oligomer assembly based on the experimental findings. The data clearly show the reciprocal relationship between dimer stability and oligomer size. However, C131-C132 involve some speculation about oligomer composition, as direct structural evidence for monomer incorporation is not provided. C133 appropriately notes implications for future structural studies.

results.result: His-104 mutants enable investigation of dimer interface effects on holdase function without pH confounds. Both mutants show enhanced holdase activity and form long-lived client complexes that are smaller and structurally distinct from oligomers alone, while WT-HSPB5 acts via weak, transient interactions, revealing two distinct mechanisms of chaperone action.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 synthesize the functional findings and identify two distinct chaperone mechanisms. The experimental design rationale (C134) is sound. The data clearly demonstrate different client-binding behaviors (C135-C138), and the mechanistic distinction (C139-C140) is well-supported by the SEC-MALS and EM data. This is a key finding revealing mechanistic diversity in sHSP function.

results.result: Disease-associated HSPB1 mutations (R127W, S135F) show stronger client interactions than WT, similar to the His-104 mutants. Previous studies identified 'high capacity' and 'low capacity' client binding modes in HSPB4. The current findings suggest that the relative strength and abundance of inter-subunit interactions affect both oligomer structure and client recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 appropriately cite relevant literature showing parallel findings in related sHSPs. C144 is a reasonable inference synthesizing the current findings with previous work. The comparison strengthens the generalizability of the findings, though the exact relationship between the different binding modes remains to be established.

results.result: Dimer interface dissociation (400 s⁻¹) is orders of magnitude faster than subunit exchange in oligomers (10⁻³ s⁻¹), indicating that breaking the dimer interface is not rate-limiting for subunit exchange. However, destabilizing the dimer yields oligomers that more readily disassemble to form stable client complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C146 compare kinetic rates and draw mechanistic conclusions. The comparison with published subunit exchange rates is appropriate. The inference that dimer dissociation is not rate-limiting for subunit exchange is well-supported. C146 is a reasonable inference based on the client-binding data, though the exact mechanism of oligomer disassembly is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Unlike plant Hsp18.1 and yeast Hsp26, which form larger complexes with clients, HSPB5 appears to have evolved to function via weak, transient interactions, with small perturbations unleashing a cryptic mode of long-lived client interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C149 compare the current findings with other sHSPs and propose an evolutionary interpretation. The cited examples (C147-C148) support the contrast. C149 is a reasonable inference about HSPB5's mechanism, though the evolutionary claim is speculative. The identification of a 'cryptic mode' is well-supported by the mutant data.

results.result: The highly charged dimer interface and Loop 5/6 provide sensitivity to small changes in pH, temperature, divalent cations, and mutations. More than half of ~20 documented disease-related mutations in sHSP ACDs occur at the dimer interface or Loop 5/6, all involving charged residue substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C151 synthesize the findings and place them in the context of disease mutations. C150 is a reasonable inference based on the structural features and experimental observations. C151 presents an analysis of known disease mutations that supports the functional importance of these regions, though the exact count and classification of mutations is not independently verified in the manuscript.

results.result: The study establishes three key insights: (1) dimer interface stability relative to other oligomer interactions modulates holdase function, with destabilization enhancing activity; (2) dimer stability can be modulated by residues outside the interface through networks of charged residues; (3) small pH changes or single mutations can shift HSPB5 between weak-transient and strong-persistent client binding modes. A continuum of oligomeric structures may enable sHSPs to modulate holdase activity as cellular conditions require.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C160 present the main conclusions and broader implications of the work. C152-C153 summarize the key findings, which are well-supported by the data. C154-C158 present three general insights that are reasonable syntheses of the findings, though C157 is somewhat speculative about the mechanism. C159 proposes a model for functional regulation that is a reasonable extrapolation from the data but remains speculative. C160 is an appropriate statement about future directions.
